title: SHA-256 from the spec
blurb: Implement the hash behind TLS certificates, git objects and Bitcoin exactly as FIPS 180-4 writes it, and check it against the published test vectors.
intro:
Do not ship hand-rolled cryptography. Use the sha2 crate, or ring, or whatever your platform already links against, because those have constant-time review, assembly paths for the SHA extensions your CPU almost certainly has, and years of people trying to break them. If you are hashing passwords, SHA-256 is the wrong primitive entirely and you want argon2 or bcrypt. This project is for understanding, and understanding is the only thing it is for.

With that said: SHA-256 is one of the most-run pieces of code on earth. Every TLS certificate chain, every git object name, every Bitcoin block header goes through it. And the whole algorithm is about sixty lines. It takes a message, pads it to a multiple of 64 bytes, and then runs each 64-byte block through 64 rounds of shuffling eight 32-bit registers, mixing in one constant and one derived word per round. There is no magic step. There is arithmetic, done carefully.

Careful is what Rust is good at here. FIPS 180-4 is written in terms of operations that are all distinct and all easy to confuse: rotate right against shift right, addition modulo 2^32 against ordinary addition, big-endian byte order against whatever your machine prefers. In C those are >>, + and a comment. In Rust each one is a named method that means exactly one thing: rotate_right, wrapping_add, to_be_bytes. Writing the wrong one is a compile error or a debug panic rather than a wrong digest you discover in production.

Four stages: the bit primitives, the padding, the compression function, and then the three test vectors NIST publishes, asserted to the character.

stages.title: The primitives, one method each
hints: `rotr` exists in this file. Look at how `big_sigma0` on the line above calls it.
`rotr` is a free function, not a method on `u32`, so it is called as `rotr(x, 6)`.

diagnose.E0599:
no method named rotr found for type u32 in the current scope.

A method call x.rotr(6) asks rustc to look for rotr in the inherent implementations of u32 and in every trait implemented for u32 that is in scope. Your pub fn rotr(x: u32, n: u32) is in neither. It is a plain function at module level, and the only way to reach it is rotr(x, 6).

The two forms are not interchangeable in Rust the way they are in some languages. impl u32 { fn rotr } is not something you can write for a type you do not own, so a free function is the right shape here. The real name for what the spec calls ROTR is u32::rotate_right, which is why rotr is a one-line wrapper: the spec's vocabulary, spelled the spec's way.
diagnose.E0308: Check the shift counts. All eight of these functions take and return u32, and the rotate and shift amounts are u32 too, so nothing here needs a cast. If you introduced a usize or a signed literal, that is the mismatch.

stages.brief: Section 4.1.2 of FIPS 180-4 defines six functions on 32-bit words, built out of rotate, shift, and, xor and not. Five of them are written. big_sigma1 is written the way the spec reads it, ROTR^6(x), and Rust does not have that method.
stages.after:
Six functions, and the whole difficulty is that they look alike. big_sigma0 and small_sigma0 differ only in three numbers and in whether the last term rotates or shifts. That last difference matters: the sigma functions used on the message schedule end in a shift, so bits fall off the end and the schedule cannot be run backwards word by word.

ch picks bit by bit, x chooses y where x is 1 and z where x is 0. maj is the bitwise majority vote of three words. Both are cheap and both are non-linear, which is the point. Xor and rotate alone would give an algorithm you could solve with linear algebra.

stages.title: Padding, and the block that does not fit
hints: `msg.len()` is a `usize`. The binding says `u64`. Rust will not widen one into the other on its own.
The cast has to happen before the multiplication, or the multiplication happens in `usize` and only then gets converted.

diagnose.E0308:
expected u64, found usize, with the annotation on the binding underlined as expected due to this.

Vec::len returns usize, the width of a pointer on this machine. u64 is exactly 64 bits everywhere. On the 64-bit machine you are probably reading this on they hold the same values, and Rust still refuses, because the two types are distinct and the code has to say which one it means.

Here that pedantry is doing real work. The spec says the length field is 64 bits, full stop. If you wrote usize and compiled for a 32-bit target, to_be_bytes would produce four bytes instead of eight, the block would be short, and every digest would be wrong. Writing as u64 pins the width to what the standard says rather than to the machine.
diagnose.E0277: Probably bits.to_be_bytes() handed straight to push rather than extend_from_slice. push takes one u8; to_be_bytes gives [u8; 8]. Pass a reference to the array and use extend_from_slice, which takes a slice of the element type.

stages.brief: The compression function eats exactly 64 bytes at a time, so the message has to be stretched to a multiple of 64 first. The recipe from section 5.1.1: append a single 1 bit (one 0x80 byte, since messages here are whole bytes), then zeros, then the message length in bits as a 64-bit big-endian integer, sized so the total lands on a block boundary. The length line will not compile.
stages.after:
The != 56 in the loop is the whole edge case. Zeros are appended until 56 bytes into a block, leaving exactly 8 for the length. A 56-byte message has no room: the 0x80 lands at offset 56, the loop cannot stop there, so it fills to 120 and the message becomes two blocks. That is why the third NIST vector is 56 bytes long. It exists specifically to catch implementations that assume one block.

The padding is also why SHA-256 is not vulnerable to trivial extension of the kind md5(secret || msg) invites in some constructions: the length is part of what gets hashed, so a message and a longer message with the same prefix pad differently. Length extension against the raw compression function is still real, which is why HMAC exists.

stages.title: The schedule and the sixty-four rounds
hints: `from_be_bytes` wants an array of exactly four bytes. A range index gives a slice, whose length the compiler does not know.
`TryInto` converts a slice to a fixed-size array at runtime, returning a `Result` because the length might not match.

diagnose.E0308:
expected [u8; 4], found &[u8], pointing at the argument.

block[a..b] is a slice. Its length lives in the value at runtime, so as far as the type system is concerned it could be any length. [u8; 4] is four bytes and the compiler knows it, which is exactly what from_be_bytes needs in order to be a compile-time reinterpretation with no bounds check.

try_into() is the bridge between the two. It compares the lengths at runtime and gives back a Result, and unwrap says you have already reasoned that the range is four wide. This is the whole slice-versus-array distinction in one line, and it is the reason Rust can hand you from_be_bytes with no error case of its own.
diagnose.E0277: If you reached for block[t * 4..t * 4 + 4].into() rather than try_into(), rustc will say the trait From<&[u8]> is not implemented for [u8; 4]. There is no infallible conversion, because a slice of the wrong length has to fail somehow. TryFrom is the version that admits it.

stages.brief: Now the core. Each 64-byte block becomes 64 words: the first sixteen are the block read big-endian, and the rest are stirred out of earlier words with the small sigmas. Then eight working registers go round 64 times, each round folding in one constant from K and one word from the schedule. The line that reads four bytes into a word does not compile.
stages.after:
Run it and the eight words print as ba7816bf 8f01cfea ..., which is the published digest of "abc" before it has even been turned into bytes. One block, and the answer is already there.

Every addition in that loop is wrapping_add. Written with +, the first block of almost any input overflows a u32 and a debug build panics with attempt to add with overflow. That panic is a feature. The spec says addition modulo 2^32, and in Rust modular addition has its own name, so an accidental overflow in code that did not intend one still gets caught. C gives unsigned overflow the same wrapping behaviour by default, which makes SHA-256 convenient and every other piece of arithmetic slightly dangerous.

The constants are not arbitrary and not chosen by anybody's taste: H0 is the first 32 bits of the fractional parts of the square roots of the first eight primes, and K the same for the cube roots of the first sixty-four. They are nothing-up-my-sleeve numbers, published so that nobody has to trust that a back door was not hidden in them.

stages.title: The three published vectors
hints: A `&u8` is a number, not a character. Something has to turn each one into two hex digits first.
`format!("{b:02x}")` produces a two-character `String` for one byte, zero padded.

diagnose.E0277:
a value of type String cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type &u8.

collect is chosen by the type it collects into, and String implements FromIterator for char, for &str, for String, and for a couple of relatives, but never for a byte. It cannot: the byte 0xba is not a character, it is a number that you want written as the two characters b and a, and only you know that hex is the encoding you meant.

Note what the error is not. Rust is not guessing wrongly about your intent, it is saying that the function you asked for does not exist. Map each byte to a String of two hex digits and collect finds FromIterator<String> for String, which concatenates.
diagnose.E0308: If you wrote digest.iter().map(|b| format!("{b:02x}")).collect::<Vec<String>>() the elements are right and the container is wrong. Either drop the turbofish and let the return type pick String, or finish with .join("").

stages.brief: Everything is in place. What is left is the loop over blocks, the eight state words serialised big-endian into 32 bytes, and a hex printer. Then the three test vectors from the NIST examples get asserted character by character: "abc", the empty string, and the 448-bit message that spills into a second block. hex does not compile.
stages.after:
Three digests, matching the values in the NIST examples exactly:

text
ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad  "abc"
e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855  ""
248d6a61d20638b8e5c026930c3e6039a33ce45964ff2167f6ecedd419db06c1  "abcdbcdecdef..."

The second one is worth a look. Hashing nothing at all still runs a full block, because padding an empty message produces 64 bytes of 0x80 and zeros, and e3b0c442... is a constant you will start recognising in git and in Docker layer digests once you know it.

What this is missing before it could be used for anything real: it is not constant-time in any audited sense, it copies the message into a fresh Vec to pad it rather than streaming, and it ignores the SHA extension instructions that make sha2 roughly ten times faster on a modern x86 or ARM core. It also has no incremental API, so hashing a large file means holding the file in memory. Those are the differences between a correct implementation and a usable one, and they are the reason the advice at the top stands.
